title: 🕵️ An engineer at OpenAI planted a listening device in a meeting room.. and secretly recorded dozens of meetings!
body: 🕵️ An engineer at OpenAI planted a listening device in a meeting room.. and secretly recorded dozens of meetings!

New US court papers have revealed that a former OpenAI engineer planted a hidden recording device behind a TV screen in an executive meeting room at the company's San Francisco headquarters, and used it to record dozens of meetings during last September.

The engineer is named Abdulrahman Al-Fozan, 35 years old, a Saudi citizen and permanent resident of the US, who had worked at the company since July 2025; he was arrested on 9 October and fired from his job on the same day.

The device is cheap and available to everyone, costing about $14 — a small electronic board carrying a microphone and a camera, which he fixed behind the TV in late September. The camera captured blurry images, but the microphone worked very well.

Investigators found more than 160 hours of audio recordings on his personal computer, and hundreds of files covering dozens of meetings held during September, in 15 folders dated from 8 to 28 September — including meetings in the executive conference room over 12 days.

Prosecutors say the recordings include what appear to be trade secrets, conversations with the company's clients, confidential legal discussions and a meeting with representatives of a foreign government. A photo of a "strategic partnership" document stamped "confidential" was also found on his phone.

Even more alarming, the engineer used the company's own coding tool, Codex, to improve his device — asking it to add a voice-detection feature so it would record speech only, and to organise the recordings into folders — through his wife's account. He also asked it about shipping boxes to Saudi Arabia and the cost of flying with five suitcases to Riyadh.

Al-Fozan pleaded not guilty on 6 November and faces a single charge of intercepting oral communications, punishable by up to five years in prison. He requested release on $1 million bail, which prosecutors oppose out of fear he may flee, and his trial is set to begin in January.
Simply put: a small $14 device and an AI tool from the company itself became a spying tool inside one of the most important AI companies in the world.
Do you trust that big companies' secrets are really protected, or do incidents like this reveal a bigger hole?
